hints: Start from the normal-incidence grating equation linking the measured $\theta$, order $n$, slit spacing $d$ and wavelength $\lambda$: $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$.
Rearrange it to match $y = \text{gradient} \times x$ with $y=n$ and $x=d\sin\theta$, and identify what combination of $\lambda$ forms the gradient.
Use that gradient expression to decide whether $\lambda$ equals the gradient itself or its reciprocal $1/\text{gradient}$.
walkthrough: Recall the diffraction grating equation for normal incidence: $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$, where $d$ is slit spacing, $\theta$ is diffraction angle and $n=0,1,2,...$.
The proposed plot uses $y=n$ and $x=d\sin\theta$, so rearrange the equation into $y=mx$ form: $n = \left(1/\lambda\right)(d\sin\theta)$.
Comparing with $y=mx$, the gradient $m$ equals $1/\lambda$ and the line passes through the origin.
Therefore the wavelength is the reciprocal of the measured gradient: $\lambda = 1/m = 1/\text{gradient}$.
Only the row with y-axis $n$, x-axis $d\sin\theta$ and wavelength $1/\text{gradient}$ matches this. This is option B.

options.A: With $y=n$ and $x=d\sin\theta$, the gradient is $1/\lambda$, not $\lambda$, so taking the gradient alone gives the reciprocal of wavelength.
options.C: Plotting $\sin\theta$ against $d/n$ does not give $y=mx$ with gradient $\lambda$ because $\sin\theta=n\lambda/d$ is not proportional to $d/n$.
options.D: Although $\sin\theta = (\lambda/d)n$, the x-axis here is $d \times n$, so the gradient would be $\lambda/d^2$, not $1/\lambda$.
